name: Nucleon decay
observables: partial-lifetime lower limits for each decay mode, for example p to e+ pi0 and p to mu+ pi0
candidate events compared with the atmospheric-neutrino background expectation
exposure in kiloton-years and fiducial volume
which decay mode a given unification model predicts to dominate
overview: Nucleon decay is the hypothetical decay of a proton, or of a neutron bound in a nucleus, into lighter particles such as a positron or a muon together with a pion. The Standard Model forbids it, but proton instability is a generic prediction of unified models of particle interactions: the review of Nath and Fileviez Perez surveys the status of proton stability in non-supersymmetric and supersymmetric grand unified theories, in extra-dimensional unification and in string and M-theory models, and lists the proposed next-generation proton-decay experiments (Hyper-Kamiokande, UNO, MEMPHYS, ICARUS, LANNDD and LENA). No decay has been observed. The Super-Kamiokande analysis of 450 kton-years of data found no candidate for p to e+ pi0 and one for p to mu+ pi0, consistent with the atmospheric-neutrino background, and set 90 % confidence-level lower limits on the partial lifetimes of 2.4 x 10^34 years (p to e+ pi0) and 1.6 x 10^34 years (p to mu+ pi0). Searches therefore need very large detector masses and long exposures deep underground.
question: Do protons and bound neutrons ever decay? Seeing even one decay would show that baryon number is not conserved and would point to a unification of the fundamental forces at very high energy.
